slide.title: Automate or Keep Human?
slide.body: A balance scale: left pan holds a small gear icon (automation), right pan holds an open hand icon (human). Small tag: AI for Freelancers · Lesson 11.

scenes.voiceover: You can now automate a step, and get AI to draft almost anything. So why not automate everything? Because one automatic message at the wrong moment can lose a client. The skill now is not building automations. It is deciding.

slide.title: What to Automate and What to Keep Human
slide.body: AI for Freelancers and Solopreneurs · Lesson 11 of 12 · Capstone step 3

scenes.voiceover: Last time, you built and tested your first automation. Now, in capstone step three, you judge every AI and automation step in your workflow.

slide.title: Question 1: How often?
slide.body: Once a year → rarely worth it · Every client, every week → strong candidate. Remember: setup and maintenance take time too.

scenes.voiceover: Ask four questions. First, how often does the task happen? A task that happens once a year is rarely worth the setup and maintenance. A task that happens for every client, every week, is a stronger candidate.

slide.title: Question 2: What if it goes wrong?
slide.body: Three-step scale, green to red: Low — small delay, easy fix · Medium — confusion, extra work · High — lost client, wrong advice, privacy problem. Arrow under it: more risk → more human checking.

scenes.voiceover: Second, what happens if it goes wrong? Rate the damage as low, like a small delay you can fix. Medium, like confusion or extra work. Or high, like a lost client, a wrong figure in advice, or a privacy problem. The higher the risk, the more human checking you need.

slide.title: Questions 3 and 4
slide.body: Q3 Personal touch? Automatic OK: confirmations, reminders · From you: advice, bad news, apologies, negotiations. Q4 Cost? Tool price + setup time + checking time + data risk, compared with time saved.

scenes.voiceover: Third, does the client expect a personal touch? Confirmations and reminders can be automatic. But advice, bad news, apologies and negotiations should come from you. Fourth, what does it cost? Count the tool price, setup time, checking time, and the risk of sharing client data with another service.

slide.title: Keep, change or remove
slide.body: Three boxes: Keep (green) · Change, e.g. Automation → AI draft I check (amber) · Remove, do by hand (grey). Below: + a one-line reason for each.

scenes.voiceover: The checklist gives one of three decisions. Keep the step as it is. Change it, for example from automation to an AI draft that you check. Or remove it, and do the task by hand. Then write a one-line reason. That reason makes your workflow trustworthy, both to you and to a client who asks how you work.

scenes.stock_query: hands folding laundry next to washing machine
scenes.voiceover: Think of a washing machine. It is excellent for the weekly laundry. But you would not put your best silk shirt, or a child's drawing, in it. The machine is not bad. Some things simply need careful hands.

scenes.stock_query: accountant meeting small business owner office
scenes.voiceover: Let's see the checklist at work. Chidi is a freelance accountant in Enugu, Nigeria. He serves about thirty small business clients, and he checks three steps in his workflow.

slide.title: Appointment reminders
slide.body: How often: many times a week · Risk: low · Personal touch: no · Cost: free option he already uses → KEEP as automation (green)

scenes.voiceover: First, appointment reminders, sent the day before each meeting. They happen many times a week. The risk is low, because the meeting is also in the client's calendar. No personal touch is expected, and it runs on a free option he already uses. Decision, keep as automation.

slide.title: Advice messages
slide.body: How often: weekly · Risk: high · Personal touch: yes, his judgement → KEEP fully human (amber). AI only to tidy his own wording, names and figures removed.

scenes.voiceover: Second, advice messages, such as what a client should do about a tax question. The risk is high, because wrong advice could cost the client money. And clients expect Chidi's own judgement. Decision, keep fully human. He may use AI only to tidy wording he has already written, with names and figures removed.

slide.title: Monthly summary notes: CHANGE
slide.body: Before, red cross: AI draft sent automatically. After, green tick: AI draft from anonymised figures → Chidi checks every figure → Chidi sends.

scenes.voiceover: Third, monthly summary notes for each client. The risk is medium to high, and clients expect a partly personal touch. Decision, change. It was an AI draft sent automatically. Now it is an AI draft from anonymised figures, checked and sent by Chidi himself.

scenes.on_screen_text: Fast where safe. Personal where it matters.
scenes.voiceover: His workflow is now faster where it is safe, and personal where it matters. He did not remove automation from his business. He put each step in the right place, and he can explain why to any client who asks.

A common mistake is to judge only by time saved. It saves twenty minutes, so I will automate it. This forgets the cost of setup, maintenance and mistakes, and the value of personal contact. But a step that sometimes sends a wrong or cold message to an important client is not a saving. Always ask all four questions.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Four questions: how often · if it goes wrong · personal touch · cost. 2. Automate repeated, low-risk, impersonal steps; keep advice and bad news human. 3. Keep, change or remove, with a reason.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, judge each AI or automation step with four questions. How often, what if it goes wrong, is a personal touch expected, and what does it cost in money, time and risk. Second, repeated, low-risk, impersonal steps suit automation, while advice, bad news and high-risk work stay human. Third, decide to keep, change or remove each step, and write a reason.

Now it is your turn, with capstone step three. Add the four questions as columns in your workflow map, and answer them for every AI and automation step. Decide keep, change or remove, with a reason, and name a human check for every high-risk step. In the final lesson, we put together your complete proposal-to-invoice workflow.
